doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

chapter: Studio years and changing rock rhythms
title: Straight eighths: The Twist on Candid Camera
summary: The shift to straight eighth rhythm, Bill Haley, and playing a Twist for Candid Camera at CBS.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: We were chatting before about later in your studio work, about playing straight eighth notes.
Well do you remember when that concept started to change? When the music started to change?

Sure, yeah. It started to change, basically, you know they called Elvis the King, right? But he didn’t play much rock & roll, they were all rhythm & blues and Shuffles and stuff like that. The King of rock & roll, but it wasn’t a lot of rock & roll. And bands like Harry so-and-so and his—
No not Harry Comet, this is the other guy, Bill —
Bill Haley and the Comets. Yeah. They were like a shuffley kind of thing.
Yeah. It wasn’t that much different from swing music.

That’s right. Then when I first started doing that and I’ll tell you, it was “The Twist,” really. You know when people do the old Chubby Checker [scats]. That kind of straight eighth rhythm was the first thing that I had to play because I was doing “Candid Camera.” We had a 15-piece band on “Candid Camera.” And Art — what’s his name?

Yeah. He comes in and the leader was a guy named Sid Raymond. And Sid was a very accomplished arranger and conductor. And so he comes in and he says, “hey we have a sequence that we can’t use their music, and we’ve got to have our own music.” He says, “do you guys know a ‘Twist’?” Everybody said no. A Twist? What the heck is a Twist? “This is a dance everybody does.” He says, “I brought a record.” So they put the record

on the PA and pumped it into the auditorium to where the band was, right? And you know that’s what it was [scats]. If I couldn’t have memorized that in five seconds I deserved to be canned. So anyway Alan Funt says to Sid Raymond he says, “Sid, do you think you can write something along those lines?” And he says, “sure.” He says, “can you have it ready by the show?” He says, “we’ll need about 45 seconds. So he says sure. So he wrote two choruses of blues, and he says, “hey Sonny, do I have to write a part for you?” I said, “no, you don’t have to write a part for me, Sid.” I says, “you’re going to play it like that, right?” He says, “yeah, that’s what it’s going to be.” So he didn’t have to write a part. So we played it on the air cold, we didn’t even rehearse it, played it on the air cold and I heard it the next week. And we used to do like three in a row or two in a row, I forget which it was. And so I heard it about two weeks later, Jesus, they pumped that in perfect. It sounded exactly like it’s supposed to. I said to my wife, “boy, can you imagine having to play like that all the time?” And that’s what it came to. They played like that all the time. That’s what you hear today. It’s all based on that. Straight eighths. And I used to, like I think I told you about that story, I used to listen to the radio going in to a recording date, and listen to what the guys were playing and try to memorize a lot of it and use it when I got to the recording date, because I wasn’t playing with those bands and I never listened to that music anyway. And that’s how that started with me. That would have been, I was at CBS for almost nine years in the 60s. So that would be in the very early 60s.
So it was like you’ve seen the writing on the wall?
